title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:reduced-boundary-domains}
		If $\Omega \subset {\mathbb R}^{n+1}$ is a bounded open set with  Ahlfors regular boundary, then it has finite perimeter.  If it also  satisfies the two-sided corkscrew condition,   then it holds that  ${\partial\Omega} = \partial_* \Omega$, (see \cite[(3.1.25),  p. 52]{HMT}).  Therefore, for such domains,   ${\mathcal H}^n(\partial \Omega \setminus \partial^* \Omega)=0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first record that, by \cite[Theorem 2.20]{CC},  the set of simple functions is dense in $L^{p,q}(\mu)$.  We will then show that for every Borel set $E \subset X$ with $\mu(E)<\infty$,  the function $\chi_E$ can be approximated by continuous functions in the $L^{p,q}(\mu)$ norm, which would imply the same result for any simple function.  To this end,  since $\mu$ is a Radon measure,  for fixed $\delta>0$ to be chosen momentarily,  there exist a compact set $K$ and an open set $U$ such that $K \subset E \subset U$ and $\mu(U \setminus K) <\delta$.  By Urysohn's lemma,  there exists $f \in C(X)$ such that $\chi_K \leq f \leq \chi_U$.  Therefore,  for fixed ${\varepsilon}>0$,  if  $\delta=\delta({\varepsilon})>0$ is the one for which \eqref{eq:absolutecontinuityLorentz} holds,  we have that 
		$$
		\| f - \chi_E\|_{L^{p,q}(\mu)} \leq \| \chi_U - \chi_E\|_{L^{p,q}(\mu)} = \| \chi_{U \setminus E}\|_{L^{p,q}(\mu)} \leq \| \chi_{U \setminus K}\|_{L^{p,q}(\mu)}<{\varepsilon}.
		$$
		We have proved that any $L^{p,q}(\mu)$ function can be approximated by continuous functions.  Since any continuous function on a compact set $X$ can be approximated by Lipschitz functions on $X$ in the uniform norm,  we readily infer that $\mathop\mathrm{Lip}(X)$  is dense in $L^{p,q}(\mu)$.  
		
		Let now $f \in L_0^{p,q}(\mu)$.   By the first part of the lemma, there exists $f_k \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}(X)$ is such that $f_k \to f$ in the $L^{p,q}(\mu)$  norm.  Since    $\| f_k -f\|_{L^{p}(\mu)}  \lesssim \| f_k-f\|_{L^{p,q}(\mu)} $, for any $p \in (1,\infty)$ and $q \in[1,p]$, we get that $\lim_{k \to \infty} f_k \to f$ in $L^1(\mu)$ and so $\fint_X f_k \,d\mu\to \fint_X f \,d\mu=0$ as $k \to \infty$. Thus,  if we set $g_k:=f_k -\fint_X f_k\,d\mu$, it is easy to see that $g_k \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}_0(X)$ and $g_k \to f$ in the $L^{p,q}(\mu)$-norm.

label: lemsr
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemsr}
		Let $\sigma$ be an $n$-dimensional Ahlfors regular measure on ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}$ and $\Sigma:=\operatorname{supp}(\sigma)$.  For $\rho\in(0,{\rm diam}(\Sigma))$, let $S_\rho$ be defined as above.
		The following holds:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item[(a)] For every $x\in\Sigma$, the kernel $s_\rho(x,\cdot)$ is supported in $\bar B(x,2\rho)$ and it holds
			$s_\rho(x,\cdot)\gtrsim \chi_{B(x,\frac14\rho)}$.
			\item[(b)] For every $x\in\Sigma$,  the kernels $s_\rho(x,\cdot)$ and $s_\rho(\cdot, x)$ are  Lipschitz on $\Sigma$, with Lipschitz constants ${\rm Lip}(s_\rho(x,\cdot))+{\rm Lip}(s_\rho(\cdot,x))\lesssim \rho^{-n-1}.$
			\item[(c)] For $1\leq p \leq\infty$, $S_\rho$ is bounded in $L^p(\sigma)$ with norm at most $1$.
			\item[(d)] For $1\leq p<\infty$ and  $f\in L^p(\sigma)$,  then $S_\rho(f)$ converges to $f$ in $L^p(\sigma)$ as $\rho\to0$.
			\item[(e)] If  $f\in L^1(\sigma)$,  then $S_\rho(f) \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}(\Sigma)$ and  ${\rm Lip}(S_\rho g) \lesssim \rho^{-n-1} \|g\|_{L^1(\sigma)}$.
		\end{itemize}

label: lemlip
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemlip}
		Let $\sigma$ be an $n$-dimensional Ahlfors regular measure on ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}$  and $\Sigma:=\operatorname{supp}(\sigma)$.  For $\rho\in(0,{\rm diam}(\Sigma))$, let $S_\rho$ be defined as above. The following hold:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item[(a)] If $g \in \dot M^{1,p}(\sigma)$, then $S_\rho g \in \dot M^{1,p}(\sigma)$ satisfying
			$$
			\|\nabla_H S_\rho g\|_{L^p(\sigma)} \lesssim \|\nabla_H  g\|_{L^p(\sigma)}.
			$$
			\item[(b)] If $g\in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}(\Sigma)$,  then $S_\rho g \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}(\Sigma)$ satisfying
			$${\rm Lip}(S_\rho g) \lesssim {\rm Lip}(g).$$
		\end{itemize}
		The implicit constants depend only on $n$ and the Ahlfors regularity constants of $\sigma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\rho\in(0,{\rm diam}(\Sigma))$.
		Let $x,x'\in\Sigma$ and suppose first that $|x-x'|\geq \rho$.
		Then we write
		$$|S_\rho g(x) - S_\rho g(x')| \leq |S_\rho g(x) -  g(x)| + |g(x) -  g(x')| + |g(x') - S_\rho g(x')|.$$
		Since $S_\rho1=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}(s_\rho(x,\cdot))\subset \bar B(x,2\rho)$,
		we have
		\begin{align*}
			|S_\rho g(x) -  g(x)| & = \bigg|\int_{\partial\Omega} s_\rho(x,y) (g(y)-g(x)))\,d\sigma(y)\bigg| \\
			& \lesssim \rho^{-n}  \int_{B(x,2\rho)} |x-y| \,\left( \nabla_H g(y) +  \nabla_H g(x) \right) \,d\sigma(y)\\
			& \lesssim \rho\, \left( {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x) +  \nabla_H g(x)\right),
		\end{align*}
		where ${\mathcal M}_\sigma$ is the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function with respect to $\sigma$. The same estimate holds with $x'$ in place of $x$. Thus,
		\begin{align*}
			|S_\rho g(x) &- S_\rho g(x')| \\
			&\lesssim  \left( {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x) +  \nabla_H g(x)+   {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x') +  \nabla_H g(x')\right)\,\rho  + |g(x) -  g(x')|\\
			& \lesssim \left( {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x) +  \nabla_H g(x)+   {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x') +  \nabla_H g(x')\right) \,|x-x'|.
		\end{align*}
		
		In case that $|x-x'|< \rho$, we write
		\begin{align*}
			S_\rho g(x) - S_\rho g(x') &= \int_{\partial\Omega} (s_\rho(x,y) - s_\rho(x',y))\,g(y)\,d\sigma(y)\\
			& =
			\int_{\partial\Omega} (s_\rho(x,y) - s_\rho(x',y))\,(g(y)-g(x))\,d\sigma(y).
		\end{align*}
		Notice that the support of the integrand is contained in
		$$\operatorname{supp}(s_\rho(x,\cdot))\cup \operatorname{supp}(s_\rho(x',\cdot))\subset 
		\bar B(x,2\rho)\cup \bar B(x',2\rho)\subset \bar B(x,3\rho).$$
		Using also that ${\mathrm Lip}(s_\rho(\cdot,y))\lesssim \rho^{-n-1}$, we deduce
		\begin{align*}
			|S_\rho g(x) - S_\rho g(x')| & \leq 
			\rho\,\int_{{\partial\Omega}\cap \bar B(x,3\rho)} |s_\rho(x,y) - s_\rho(x',y)|\,\,\left( \nabla_H g(y) +  \nabla_H g(x) \right) \,d\sigma(y)\\
			&\lesssim \rho \, \frac{|x-x'|}{\rho^{n+1}}\int_{{\partial\Omega}\cap \bar B(x,3\rho)}\left( \nabla_H g(y) +  \nabla_H g(x) \right)  \,\,d\sigma(y)\\
			&\lesssim |x-x'| \,\left( {\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)(x) +  \nabla_H g(x)\right).
		\end{align*}
		Hence, $C({\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g) +  \nabla_H g)$ is an upper gradient of $g$ with $L^p(\sigma)$ norm bounded above by $C'\|\nabla_Hg\|_{L^p(\sigma)}$.
		This completes the proof of (a). 
		
		To prove (b), one readily checks that in the case that $g \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}(\Sigma)$, the above estimates
		hold replacing $\nabla_H g$ and ${\mathcal M}_\sigma(\nabla_H  g)$ by $\mathop\mathrm{Lip}(g)$.

If $f \in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}({\partial\Omega})$, then Lemma \ref{lem:HMT vs Hajlasz}  follows from  \cite[eq. (4.15)]{MT} and  \cite[Lemma 6.3]{MT},  where the implicit constants are independent of the Lipschitz constant of $f$.  Let us now assume that $f \in M^{1,p}({\partial\Omega})$ and let ${\varphi} \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb R}^{n+1})$. By Lemma \ref{lemsr} (d) and (e),  H\"older's inequality,  \eqref{eq:M emb W} for Lipschitz functions,  and  Lemma \ref{lemlip} (a), we obtain 
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial^* \Omega} f \,\partial_{t, k, j} {\varphi} \,d\sigma_*&= \lim_{\rho \to 0}\int_{\partial^* \Omega} S_\rho f \,\partial_{t, k, j} {\varphi} \,d\sigma_*=\lim_{\rho \to 0}\int_{\partial^* \Omega} \partial_{t, j, k} S_\rho f\, {\varphi} \,d\sigma_*\\
			& \leq \lim_{\rho \to 0} \|\partial_{t, j, k} S_\rho f\|_{L^p(\partial^* \Omega)} \, \| {\varphi} \|_{L^{p'}(\partial^* \Omega)} \\
			& \leq \lim_{\rho \to 0} \|\nabla_H S_\rho f\|_{L^p(\partial \Omega)} \, \| {\varphi} \|_{L^{p'}(\partial ^*\Omega)} \lesssim  \|\nabla_H  f\|_{L^p(\partial \Omega)} \, \| {\varphi} \|_{L^{p'}(\partial^* \Omega)},
		\end{align*}
		which, by the definition of $W^{1,p}(\partial^* \Omega)$,  concludes the proof of the lemma.

label: eq:tang.der.bound n.t. maximal
title: Proof
body_md:
We will only prove the  statements involving the Lorentz spaces,  as the others are similar and slightly easier.
		Suppose first that $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p})_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable with constant $C_4$ and let us check that then $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}})_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable with constant $\lesssim C_4$.
		Let $j,k,u,g$ be as in {(\ref{eqdualneumann})} with ${\mathcal L}^* $ and $A^T$  in place of ${\mathcal L}$ and $A$ and consider an arbitrary function ${\varphi}\in \mathop\mathrm{Lip}({\partial\Omega}) \cap L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})$.
		Let $v:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the solution of the Neumann problem with boundary data ${\varphi}-m_{\sigma,{\partial\Omega}}{\varphi}$. Using that $m_{\sigma,{\partial\Omega}}(u)=0$, we get
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma &= \int_{\partial\Omega} u\,({\varphi}-m_{\sigma,{\partial\Omega}}{\varphi})\,d\sigma =
			\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,\partial_{\nu_A} v\,d\sigma = \int_\Omega A\nabla u\cdot \nabla v\,dm\\
			& = \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{\nu_{A^T}} u\, v\,d\sigma
			= \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k} g\, v\,d\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} g\, \partial_{t,k,j}  v\,d\sigma.
		\end{align*} 
		As usual, abusing notation we denoted by $u$ the  trace of $u$ on ${\partial\Omega}$.
		Therefore,  by Lemma \ref{lem:HMT vs Hajlasz} and a standard argument originating from \cite{Kenig-Pipher} (see for instance \cite[Eq. (4.3.11)]{HMT}), we have that
		\begin{align}\label{eq:tang.der.bound n.t. maximal}
			\left|\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma\right| & \lesssim \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|\partial_{t,k,j}  v\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim\|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|\nabla_H v\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})}\\
			&\lesssim \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|{\mathcal N}_\Omega(\nabla  v)\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})} \notag \\
			& \leq C_4\|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|\partial_{\nu_A} v\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})} = C_4\|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|{\varphi}\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})} \notag
		\end{align}
		By Lemma \ref{lem:denseLorentz} and  {(\ref{eqclau29})}, we infer that
		$$\|u\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim C_4 \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}.$$
		Next,  since $(R_q)_{{\mathcal L}}$  is solvable for ${\mathcal L}$ some $q>p$,  by Theorem \cite[Theorem 1.6]{MT}, we deduce that  the Dirichlet problem is solvable for ${\mathcal L}^*$ in $L^{q'}({\partial\Omega})$. Hence, by interpolation,  the Dirichlet problem is also solvable from $L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})$ to $L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})$ and so
		$$\|{\mathcal N}_\Omega(u)\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim \|u\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim C_4 \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})},$$
		concluding that $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}})_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable.
		
		
		
		Suppose now that $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}})_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable with constant $C_*$ and let us prove that  $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p})_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable with constant $\lesssim C_*$.
		Let $u$ be solution of the Neumann problem in $\Omega$ with boundary data $\partial_{\nu_A} u=f$ for some $f\in L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega}) \cap L_0^{2n/(n+1)}({\partial\Omega})$.  Since ${\partial\Omega}$ satisfies a weak $p$-Poincar\'e inequality,  then,   by \cite[Theorem 1.6]{GMT} and \cite[Lemma 1.3]{MT},  it also holds that $(R_p)_{\mathcal L}$\footnote{We mean the regularity problem in terms of the tangential derivatives. Notice however that, since ${\partial\Omega}$ supports a Poincar\'e inequality, this is equivalent to the regularity problem in the Haj\l asz space $\dot M^{1,p}({\partial\Omega})$. See \cite[Lemma 1.3]{MT} for more details.} is solvable. Thus, it suffices to show that for all $1\leq j,k\leq n+1$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eqdual1}
			\|\partial_{t,j,k} u\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})} \leq C_*\,\|f\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})},
		\end{equation}
		where again $u$ on ${\partial\Omega}$ should be understood as a trace.
		To this end, consider an arbitrary function  $\psi\in L^{p'}({\partial\Omega}) \cap \mathop\mathrm{Lip}({\partial\Omega})$ and let $w:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the solution of the
		rough Neumann problem for ${\mathcal L}^*$ with data $\partial_{\nu_{A^T}} w= \partial_{t,k,j}\psi$.
		Then we have
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k} u\,\psi\,d\sigma &= \int_{\partial\Omega}  u\,\partial_{t,k,j}\psi\,d\sigma   
			=\int_{\partial\Omega} u\, \partial_{\nu_{A^T}} w\,d\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{\nu_A} u\,  w\,d\sigma 
			\\
			&\leq \| \partial_{\nu_A} u\|_{L^{p,1}(\Omega)}\,\|w\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})}\leq C_*\,\| f\|_{L^{p,1}(\Omega)}\,\|\psi\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})},
		\end{align*}
		which gives {(\ref{eqdual1})} by density and duality.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $1<p<\infty$, $\rho\in (0,{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega}))$, and let $\Omega$ be a bounded chord-arc domain.
		Suppose that the Dirichlet problem for ${\mathcal L}^*$ is solvable in $L^{p'}$ and in $L^{p',\infty}$.
		Then $(N_p(\rho))_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable if and only if $(N^R_{p'}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable. Also, 
		$(N_{L^{p,1},L^p}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}}$ is solvable if and only if $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable.
		Further, 
		$$C_{\mathcal L}(N_p(\rho))\approx C_{{\mathcal L}^*}(N^R_{p'}(\rho) )\qquad \text{and}\qquad C_{\mathcal L}(N_{L^{p,1},L^p}(\rho))\approx C_{{\mathcal L}^*}(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}}(\rho)).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The arguments are very similar to the ones for Proposition \ref{propodual1}.  However, we show the details for completeness.
		We will only prove the second statement since the first one is similar. 
		
		
		Suppose  that $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p}(\rho))_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable with constant $C_4$.  We will check that $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable with constant $\lesssim C_4$ as well.
		Let $j,k,u,g,\rho$ be as in {(\ref{eqdualneumannsmooth})} with ${\mathcal L}^*$ and $A^T$ in place of ${\mathcal L}$ and $A$ and consider an arbitrary function ${\varphi}\in L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})\cap \mathop\mathrm{Lip}({\partial\Omega})$.
		Let $v:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the solution of the Neumann problem for ${\mathcal L}$ with boundary data ${\varphi}-m_{\sigma,{\partial\Omega}}{\varphi}$. Then, we have that
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma &= \int_{\partial\Omega} u\,({\varphi}-m_{\sigma,{\partial\Omega}}{\varphi})\,d\sigma =
			\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,\partial_{\nu_A} v\,d\sigma \\
			& = \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{\nu_{A^T}} u\, v\,d\sigma
			= \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho(g)\, v\,d\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} g\, S_\rho(\partial_{t,k,j}  v)\,d\sigma.
		\end{align*} 
		Therefore,
		\begin{align*}
			\left|\int_{\partial\Omega} u\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma\right| & \lesssim \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|S_\rho(\partial_{t,k,j}  v)\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})}
			\\
			& \leq C_4\|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|\partial_{\nu_A} v\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})} = C_4\|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}\, \|{\varphi}\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})},
		\end{align*}
		where $C_4$ is the constant of $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p})$.   By density and duality,  we deduce that
		$$\|u\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim C_4 \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}.$$
		Using  that the  Dirichlet problem is solvable from $L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})$ to $L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})$,  we infer that
		$$\|{\mathcal N}_\Omega(u)\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim \|u\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim C_4 \|g\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})}.$$
		That is, $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable with constant $\lesssim C_4$.
		
		Suppose now that $(N^R_{L^{p'},L^{p',\infty}}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}^*}$ is solvable with constant $C_*$ and let us prove that then $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p}(\rho))_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable with constant $\lesssim C_*$.
		Let $u$ be solution of $(N_{L^{p,1},L^p}(\rho))_{\mathcal L}$ with boundary data $\partial_{\nu_A} u=f$, for some $f\in L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega}) \cap \mathop\mathrm{Lip}_0({\partial\Omega})$.  We aim to show that for all $1\leq j,k\leq n+1$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eqdual1'}
			\|S_\rho(\partial_{t,j,k} u)\|_{L^p({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim C_*\,\|f\|_{L^{p,1}({\partial\Omega})}.
		\end{equation}
		To this end, consider an arbitrary Lipschitz function $\psi\in L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})$ and let $w:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the solution of the
		rough Neumann problem for ${\mathcal L}^*$ with $\partial_{\nu_{A^T}} w= \partial_{t,k,j}S_\rho(\psi)$.
		Then we have
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial\Omega} S_\rho(\partial_{t,j,k} u)\,\psi\,d\sigma &= \int_{\partial\Omega}  u\,\partial_{t,k,j}S_\rho(\psi)\,d\sigma   
			=\int_{\partial\Omega} u\, \partial_{\nu_{A^T}} w\,d\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{\nu_A} u\,  w\,d\sigma 
			\\
			&\leq \| \partial_{\nu_A} u\|_{L^{p,1}(\Omega)}\,\|w\|_{L^{p',\infty}({\partial\Omega})}\leq C_*\,\| f\|_{L^{p,1}(\Omega)}\,\|\psi\|_{L^{p'}({\partial\Omega})},
		\end{align*}
		which gives {(\ref{eqdual1'})} by  duality.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the variational solution of  {(\ref{eqdualneumannsmooth})}. Then
		$$u(x) = \int_{\partial\Omega} N(x,y)\,\partial_{t,j,k} (S_\rho g)(y)\,d\sigma(y).$$
		For brevity, we write
		$$u= N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} (S_\rho g)).$$
		From the properties of the kernel of $S_\rho$ in Lemma \ref{lemsr} and Schur's lemma, it follows that $\partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho$ is an operator bounded in $L^{p}(\sigma)$ with norm $\lesssim \rho^{-1}$, for $1\leq p\leq\infty$. On the other hand, since
		$$\int_{{\partial\Omega}}N(x,y)\,d\sigma(y)\lesssim \int_{{\partial\Omega}}\frac1{|x-y|^{n-1}}\,d\sigma(y)\lesssim {\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$$
		and the same estimate holds for $N(y,x)$, by Schur's criterion again, we deduce that the operator $N_\sigma$ is bounded in $L^{p}(\sigma)$ with norm
		$\lesssim {\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$.
		Therefore,
		$$\|u\|_{L^{p}(\sigma)} = \|N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} (S_\rho g))\|_{L^{p}(\sigma) }\lesssim {\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})\,
		\|\partial_{t,j,k} (S_\rho g))\|_{L^{p}(\sigma)} \lesssim \frac{{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})}\rho\,\|g\|_{L^{p}({\partial\Omega})}.$$

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemuniformrho}
		Let $\Omega\subset{\mathbb R}^{n+1}$ be a bounded chord-arc domain and suppose that $(D_{p})_{{\mathcal L}}$ is solvable for some $p\in(1,\infty)$.   Then $(N^R_{p})_{\mathcal L}$ is solvable if and only if $(N^R_{p}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}}$ is solvable uniformly on $0<\rho\leq{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that  $(N^R_{p})$ is solvable and let $0<\rho\leq{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$.
		For $g\in L^{p}({\partial\Omega})$, let $u_\rho:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the variational solution of {(\ref{eqdualneumannsmooth})}.
		Then, by the solvability of $(N^R_{p})$ and the $L^{p}(\sigma)$ boundedness of $S_\rho$ with norm $1$,
		$$\|{\mathcal N}_\Omega(u_\rho)\|_{L^{p}({\partial\Omega})} \lesssim \|S_\rho g\|_{L^{p}({\partial\Omega})}\leq\| g\|_{L^{p}({\partial\Omega})}
		.$$
		So $(N^R_{p}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}}$ is solvable uniformly on $0<\rho\leq{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$.
		
		Conversely, suppose that $(N^R_{p}(\rho))_{{\mathcal L}}$ is solvable uniformly on $0<\rho\leq{\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$.
		For $g\in L^{p}({\partial\Omega})\cap \mathop\mathrm{Lip}({\partial\Omega})$,  let $u$ and $u_\rho:\Omega\to{\mathbb R}$ be the respective variational solutions of 
		{(\ref{eqdualneumann})} and {(\ref{eqdualneumannsmooth})}. 
		We claim that $u$ and $u_\rho$ are continuous in $\overline \Omega$ and
		$u_\rho$ converges to $u$ in $L^{p}(\sigma)$ as $\rho\to0$. Together with the $L^{p}$ solvability of the Dirichlet problem, this implies that 
		$$\|{\mathcal N}_\Omega(u)\|_{L^{p}({\partial\Omega})}\lesssim\|u\|_{L^{p}(\sigma)} = \lim_{\rho\to 0}\|u_\rho\|_{L^{p}(\sigma)}\leq C\,\|g\|_{L^p(\sigma)},$$
		which completes the proof of the lemma, modulo our claim.
		
		To prove the claim, observe first that, from the fact that $g$ is Lipschitz, by Lemma \ref{lemlip}, it follows that
		$S_\rho g$ is also Lipschitz uniformly on $\rho$. Hence, $\partial_{t,j,k} g$ and  $\partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho g$ are 
		in $L^\infty(\sigma)$ uniformly in $\rho$. Arguing as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemfinit},  it follows that
		$N_\sigma$ is bounded in 
		$L^{\infty}(\sigma)$ (with norm depending on ${\rm diam}({\partial\Omega})$), and so $u = N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} g)$ and $u_\rho 
		= N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho g)$ are uniformly in $L^\infty(\sigma)$. By the H\"older continuity of the Neumann function away from the diagonal given by Theorem  \ref{teoneumann1} (vi) and the local integrability implied by (v) in the same theorem, using standard arguments, it follows that 
		in fact, $u$ and $u_\rho$ are continuous in $\overline\Omega$. 
		
		
		By the dominated convergence theorem, since $u_\rho$ and $u$ are uniformly in $L^\infty(\sigma)$, to prove the convergence of $u_\rho$ to $u$ in $L^{p}(\sigma)$, it suffices to check that $u_\rho$ converges to $u$ pointwise in ${\partial\Omega}$.
		First we check the weak convergence of $\partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho g$ to $\partial_{t,j,k} g$ in $L^{q}(\sigma)$, for all $q\in (1,\infty)$. Indeed, if ${\varphi}$ is a  $C^1$ function in a neighborhood of ${\partial\Omega}$, then
		\begin{equation}\label{eqconv61}
			\int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k}(S_\rho g)\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma = \int_{\partial\Omega} S_\rho(g)\,\partial_{t,k,j}{\varphi}\,d\sigma\to 
			\int_{\partial\Omega} g\,\partial_{t,k,j}{\varphi}\,d\sigma=\int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k}g\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma \quad \mbox{ as $\rho\to0$,}
		\end{equation}
		because $S_\rho(g)$ converges to $g$ in $L^q(\sigma)$. Since the $L^q(\sigma)$ norms of $\partial_{t,j,k}(S_\rho g)$ and 
		$\partial_{t,j,k}g$ are bounded uniformly in $L^q(\sigma)$, {(\ref{eqconv61})} also holds for any ${\varphi}\in L^{q'}(\sigma)$, by density.
		That is, $\partial_{t,j,k} S_\rho g$ converges to $\partial_{t,j,k} g$ weakly in $L^{q}(\sigma)$ as $\rho\to0$.
		
		Finally, from the fact that $N^x\equiv N(x,\cdot)\in L^q(\sigma)$ for $1<q<n/(n-1)$, we deduce that, for any $x\in\overline\Omega$,
		$$
		N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} (S_\rho g))(x) = \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k}S_\rho(g)\,N^x\,d\sigma \to  \int_{\partial\Omega} \partial_{t,j,k} g\,N^x\,d\sigma=
		N_\sigma(\partial_{t,j,k} g)(x),\,\,\textup{as}\,\,\rho \to 0.
		$$
		This finishes the proof of the claim.

Notice that {(\ref{eqtyp45})} follows from {(\ref{eqtyp450})} setting ${\varphi}=1$.
		
		To prove {(\ref{eqtyp450})}, let $E=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, consider a decomposition of $\Omega$ into Whitney cubes as in Section \ref{secwhitney}, and  denote by ${\mathcal W}_0$ the family of the Whitney cubes that intersect $B_0\cap E$. Reducing the size of the Whitney cubes if necessary, we can assume that
		$P\subset 1.5 B_0$ for each $P\in {\mathcal W}_0$.
		By monotone convergence and the inner regularity of $\mu$,  we can also assume that 
		${\rm dist}(E,{\partial\Omega})>0$, which implies that the family ${\mathcal W}_0$ is finite. 
		
		By the lower Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}$ and the properties of Whitney cubes, we can choose positive constants $C_6$ (depending on $n$) and
		$\tau$ (depending on $n$ and the Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}$) such that
		for each $P\in{\mathcal W}_0$, the ball ${\widetilde{B}}(P) :=B(x_P,C_6\ell(P))$ (where $x_P$ is the center of $P$) satisfies 
		$3P\subset {\widetilde{B}}(P)$ and 
		\begin{equation}\label{eqsig840}
			\sigma({\widetilde{B}}(P)\cap B_0\cap{\partial\Omega}) \geq \tau\,\ell(P)^n
		\end{equation}
		(in particular, this implies that ${\widetilde{B}}(P)\cap B_0\cap{\partial\Omega}\neq\varnothing$).
		For later reference, notice that the growth conditions on $\mu$ ensures that
		\begin{equation}\label{eqsig841}
			\mu({\widetilde{B}}(P))\lesssim \mu(3P) \leq C_0'\,\ell(P)^n,
		\end{equation}
		with $C_0'$ depending only on $\bar C_0$ and $n$.
		
		We claim that for each \( P \in {\mathcal W}_0 \), we can choose a Borel subset \( F_P \subset {\widetilde{B}}(P) \cap 2B_0 \cap \partial \Omega \) such that there exist constants \( c_2 > 0 \) and \( A > 1 \), depending on \( n \), the Ahlfors regularity of \( \partial \Omega \), and \( \bar{C}_0 \), for which the following holds:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item[(a)] $c_2\mu(3P)\leq \sigma(F_P) \leq \mu(3P)$, and
			\item[(b)] $\sum_{P\in{\mathcal W}_0}\chi_{F_P}\leq (A+1)\,\chi_{2B_0}.$
		\end{itemize}
		
		Assume the claim for the moment, and let us see how the lemma follows.  From the fact that $F_P\subset {\widetilde{B}}(P)\cap 2B_0\cap{\partial\Omega}$, we have
		$$P\subset \gamma_\Omega(\xi)\cap 2B_0 \quad\mbox{ for $\xi\in F_P$,}$$
		where $\gamma_\Omega(\xi)$ is a non-tangential cone associated with ${\mathcal N}_\Omega$ with vertex at $\xi$, with aperture  large enough. Thus
		$$u(x)\leq \inf_{\xi\in F_P} {\mathcal N}_{\Omega,4r(B_0)}(u)(\xi)\quad\mbox{ for all $x\in P\cap E$.}$$
		From this fact, the properties (a), (b) claimed above, and {(\ref{eqsig841})}, we deduce 
		\begin{align*}
			\int |u\,{\varphi}|\,d\mu & = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal W}_0}\int_{P} |u\,{\varphi}|\,d\mu 
			\leq \sum_{P\in{\mathcal W}_0}\inf_{\xi\in F_P} {\mathcal N}_{\Omega,4r(B_0)}(u)(\xi)\,\int_{{\widetilde{B}}(P)}|{\varphi}|\,d\mu\\
			&  \lesssim \sum_{P\in{\mathcal W}_0}\inf_{\xi\in F_P} \big( {\mathcal N}_{\Omega,4r(B_0)}(u)(\xi)\,{\mathcal M}_\mu({\varphi})(\xi)\big)\,\mu(3P)\\
			& \lesssim
			\sum_{P\in{\mathcal W}_0}\int_{F_P} {\mathcal N}_{\Omega,4r(B_0)}(u)\,{M}_\mu({\varphi})\,d\sigma \lesssim A\int_{2B_0} {\mathcal N}_{\Omega,4r(B_0)}(u)\,{{\mathcal M}}_\mu({\varphi})\,d\sigma,
		\end{align*}
		which proves {(\ref{eqtyp450})}.
		{\vspace{2mm}}
		
		Next we prove the claim. To this end, since ${\mathcal W}_0$ is a finite family, we can order it so that
		${\mathcal W}_0=\{P_1,P_2,\ldots P_{N}\}$, with $\ell(P_i)\leq \ell(P_{i+1})$ for all $i=1,\ldots,N-1$.
		We will construct the sets $F_i\equiv F_{P_i}$ inductively, 
		checking that for each $i=1,\ldots,N$ it holds
		\begin{equation}\label{eqind497}
			F_i\subset {\widetilde{B}}(P_i)\cap 2B_0\cap{\partial\Omega} =:S_i,
		\end{equation}
		and moreover,
		\begin{equation}\label{eqind498}
			c_2\,\mu(3P_i)\leq \sigma(F_i) \leq \mu(3P_i)
		\end{equation}
		and
		\begin{equation}\label{eqind499}
			\sum_{k=1}^i\chi_{F_k}\leq (A+1)\,\chi_{2B_0},
		\end{equation}
		with $c_2=\tau/(2C_0')$ and some sufficiently large $A>1$.
		
		To start, we choose an arbitrary Borel set $F_1\subset S_1= {\widetilde{B}}(P_1)\cap 2B_0\cap{\partial\Omega}$ satisfying {(\ref{eqind498})}. The existence of
		$F_1$ is ensured by the fact that, by {(\ref{eqsig840})} and 
		{(\ref{eqsig841})}, for each $P_i$ it holds
		\begin{equation}\label{eqsigh23}
			\sigma(S_i) \geq \tau\,\ell(P_i)^n \geq \tau\,\mu(3P_i)/C_0'.
		\end{equation}
		Recall that $S_i={\widetilde{B}}(P_i)\cap B_0\cap{\partial\Omega}$.
		Obviously, {(\ref{eqind499})} also holds.
		
		Suppose now that we have already constructed sets $F_1,\ldots,F_i$ satisfying 
		{(\ref{eqind497})}, {(\ref{eqind498})}, and {(\ref{eqind499})}, and let us construct $F_{i+1}$ for $i\leq N$.
		For any $\lambda>0$, by Chebyshev's inequality,  we have
		\begin{align*}
			T:=\sigma\Big(\Big\{x\in S_{i+1}:\sum_{1\leq k\leq i} \chi_{F_k}(x)>\lambda\Big\}\Big)
			\leq \frac1\lambda\sum_{1\leq k\leq i} \sigma(F_k \cap S_{i+1}).
		\end{align*}
		Notice now that if $F_k \cap S_{i+1}\neq\varnothing$, then ${\widetilde{B}}(P_k)\cap {\widetilde{B}}(P_{i+1})\neq\varnothing$, and then
		$3P_k\subset {\widetilde{B}}(P_k)\subset 3 {\widetilde{B}}(P_{i+1})$, since $r({\widetilde{B}}(P_k))\leq r({\widetilde{B}}(P_{i+1}))$ for $k<i+1$. So, if we denote by $I_{i+1}$ the subset of indices
		$k$ with $1\leq k\leq i$ such that $F_k \cap S_{i+1}\neq\varnothing$, using the upper estimate in {(\ref{eqind498})}, we get
		$$T
		\leq \frac1\lambda\sum_{k\in I_{i+1}} \sigma(F_k \cap S_{i+1}) \leq
		\frac1\lambda\sum_{k\in I_{i+1}}  \mu(3P_k)\leq \frac C\lambda  \mu(3 {\widetilde{B}}(P_{i+1}))
		.$$
		By the upper growth condition on $\mu$, we deduce
		$$T\leq \frac{c\,\bar C_0}\lambda\,\ell(P_{i+1})^n,
		$$
		with $\bar C_0$ as in {(\ref{eqtyp4500})}.
		
		So choosing $A=\lambda=\frac{2c\bar C_0}\tau$, by {(\ref{eqsig840})}, we derive
		$$\sigma\Big(\Big\{x\in S_{i+1}:\sum_{1\leq k\leq i} \chi_{F_k}(x)>A\Big\}\Big) \leq
		\frac\tau2\,\ell(P_{i+1})^n\leq \frac12\,\sigma(S_{i+1}).$$
		Then we can take a subset 
		$$F_{i+1}\subset \Big\{x\in S_{i+1}:\sum_{1\leq k\leq i} \chi_{F_k}(x)\leq A\Big\}$$
		satisfying
		$$\sigma(F_{i+1}) =\min\big(\mu(3P_{i+1}),\,\tfrac12\sigma(S_{i+1})\big).$$
		So either $\sigma(F_{i+1}) =\mu(3P_{i+1})$ or 
		$$\sigma(F_{i+1}) =\frac12\sigma(S_{i+1}) \geq \frac{C_0'^{-1}\tau}2\,\mu(3P_{i+1}),
		$$
		using {(\ref{eqsigh23})} in the last inequality. So in any case $F_{i+1}$ satisfies the required properties 
		{(\ref{eqind497})}, {(\ref{eqind498})}, {(\ref{eqind499})}, and then the claim follows.

\noindent {\bf Existence of $\partial_{\nu_A} w$ and proof of {(\ref{eqnatural3*})}.}
		First we check that the conormal derivative $\partial_{\nu_A} w$ exists locally in ${\partial\Omega}\cap 2B$ in the weak sense and it belongs to $L^q(\sigma|_{2B})$. 
		Let ${\varphi}:{\partial\Omega}\to{\mathbb R}$ be a Lipschitz function supported on $2B\cap{\partial\Omega}$,  extend it to a Lipschitz function in $\Omega$, which we still denote by ${\varphi}$, so that it vanishes in $\Omega\setminus 3B$,  and define
		$$T_w({\varphi}) = \int_\Omega A\nabla w \cdot\nabla{\varphi}\,dm.$$
		Using the fact that ${\mathcal L} w =0$ in $3B$, it easily follows  that the definition does not depend on the precise extension of ${\varphi}$.
		
		To check that $T_w$  extends to a bounded functional in $L^{q'}(\sigma|_{2B})$, consider a partition
		of $\Omega$ into a family ${\mathcal W}(\Omega)$ of dyadic Whitney cubes as in Section \ref{secwhitney}, and let $\Omega_k$ be the interior of the closure of the cubes from ${\mathcal W}(\Omega)$ with side length at least $2^{-k}$.
		From the fact that ${\mathcal N}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\nabla w)\in L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})$ (where ${\widetilde{\sigma}}$ is the surface measure on $\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}$),
		it follows that $\nabla w\in L^q({\widetilde{\Omega}})$, and thus by dominated convergence,
		$$T_w({\varphi}) = \lim_{k\to\infty}\int_{\Omega_k} A\nabla w \cdot\nabla{\varphi}\,dm.$$
		Since $\nabla w$ is uniformly continuous in $\Omega\cap 3B$  with modulus of continuity $\theta(t):=\int_0^t \omega_A(r)\,\frac{dr}r$ (by \cite{DK}), we can use the divergence theorem in \cite[Theorem 2.8]{HMT} applied to $\Omega_k$ and ${\varphi} A\nabla w$
		to derive
		$$\int_{\Omega_k} {\rm div}({\varphi} A\nabla w)\,dm =
		\int_{\partial\Omega_k} {\varphi} A\nabla w\cdot\nu\,d{\mathcal H}^n.$$
		Indeed, the assumptions in that theorem hold, since in the sense of distributions ${\rm div}({\varphi} A\nabla w) = \nabla{\varphi} A\nabla w$ is continuous in a neighborhood of $\overline{\Omega_k}$ (because
		$A$ is continuous\footnote{In fact, in any compact set, $A$ agrees a.e.\ with a uniformly continuous function.}, and $\nabla{\varphi}$ and $\nabla w|_{3B}$ are continuous), and also ${\mathcal N}_{\Omega_k}({\varphi} A\nabla w)\in L^p({\mathcal H}^n|_{{\partial\Omega}_k})$ and the pointwise non-tangential trace of ${\varphi} A\nabla w|_{{\partial\Omega}_k}$ exists, using again the continuity of $A$ and of $\nabla w$ in a neighborhood of $\overline{\Omega_k}$.  
		Then we have
		\begin{align*}
			|T_w({\varphi})| &\leq \limsup_{k\to\infty}\bigg|\int_{\Omega_k} {\rm div}({\varphi} A\nabla w)\,dm\bigg| =
			\limsup_{k\to\infty}\bigg|\int_{\partial\Omega_k} {\varphi} A\nabla w\cdot\nu_{\Omega_k}\,d{\mathcal H}^n\bigg|\\
			& \lesssim \limsup_{k\to\infty}\int_{\partial\Omega_k\cap 2B} |{\varphi}\,\nabla w|\,d{\mathcal H}^n.
		\end{align*}
		Now we intend to apply Lemma \ref{lemaux2}
		with  $\mu_k={\mathcal H}^n|_{{\partial\Omega}_k\cap{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ and ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$ in place of $\Omega$. Remark that the maximal operator  ${\mathcal M}_{\mu_k}$ is bounded from $L^{q'}(\mu_k)$ to $L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})$. Indeed,  for any $f\in L^{q'}(\mu_k)$ and $x\in{\mathbb R}^{n+1}$, by the Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}_k$ (implied by the Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}$), we have
		$${\mathcal M}_{\mu_k}(f)(x)\lesssim \sup_{r>0} \frac1{r^n}\,\int_{B(x,r)}|f|\,d\mu_k=: {\mathcal M}_n(f)(x).$$
		Using the Ahlfors regularity (or just the polynomial growth) of ${\widetilde{\sigma}}$, it follows easily that ${\mathcal M}_n$ is bounded from $L^1(\mu_k)$ to
		$L^{1,\infty}({\widetilde{\sigma}})$. Also, it is immediate that ${\mathcal M}_{\mu_k}$ is bounded from $L^\infty(\mu_k)$ to $L^\infty({\widetilde{\sigma}})$. By interpolation then, it is bounded in from $L^{q'}(\mu_k)$ to $L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})$.
		
		Using also the  solvability of $(N_q)_{\mathcal L}$ in ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$ and {(\ref{eqgradpunt})}, we can now use Lemma \ref{lemaux2} to get
		\begin{align*}
			|T_w({\varphi})|&\lesssim \limsup_{k\to\infty}\int_{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}} {\mathcal N}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\nabla w)\,{\mathcal M}_{\mu_k}({\varphi})\,d{\widetilde{\sigma}}\\
			&\lesssim {\widetilde{C}}_q\,\|\partial_{{\widetilde{\nu}}_A}w\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\,\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|{\mathcal M}_{\mu_k}({\varphi})\|_{L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\lesssim{\widetilde{C}}_q\,
			\|\psi_0\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\,\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|{\varphi}\|_{L^{q'}(\mu_k)}.
		\end{align*}
		Using that ${\varphi}$ is a Lipschitz function in $\overline{\Omega}$, it follows easily that
		$\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|{\varphi}\|_{L^{q'}(\mu_k)}\lesssim \|{\varphi}\|_{L^{q'}(\sigma)}.$
		Consequently, $$|T_w({\varphi})|\lesssim {\widetilde{C}}_q\,\|\partial_{{\widetilde{\nu}}_A}w\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\,\|{\varphi}\|_{L^{q'}(\sigma)},$$ and
		by the Hahn-Banach theorem, $T_w$ extends to a bounded functional in $L^{q'}(\sigma|_{2B})$, as wished. Then, by the Riesz representation theorem, there exists some function 
		$g\in L^{q}(\sigma|_{2B})$ such that
		$$\int_\Omega A\nabla w \cdot\nabla{\varphi}\,dm = T_w({\varphi}) = \int_{{\partial\Omega}} g\,{\varphi}\,d\sigma$$
		for any Lipschitz function ${\varphi}:{\partial\Omega}\to{\mathbb R}$ supported on $2B\cap{\partial\Omega}$, whose Lipschitz extension is supported in $3B$, and moreover
		$$\|g\|_{L^{q}(\sigma|_{2B})} = \|T_w\|_{L^{q}(\sigma|_{2B})\to{\mathbb R}} \lesssim {\widetilde{C}}_q\,\|\psi_0\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})},$$
		which proves {(\ref{eqnatural3*})}.
		
		{\vspace{2mm}}
		\noindent {\bf Proof of {(\ref{eqnatural1*})}.} 
		                                                                            
		                                 
		                                                                                                                                                                
		               
		                                                                 
		The $n$-rectifiability and $n$-Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ also
		implies the existence of tangents ${\mathcal H}^n$-a.e.\ in ${\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$. That is, for any ${\mathcal H}^n$-a.e.\  $\xi\in{\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ there exists a hyperplane $L_\xi$ through $\xi$ such that following holds. For any $\theta\in (0,1)$, there exists $r(\xi,\theta)>0$ such that
		\begin{equation}\label{eqtan5}
			({\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}})\cap B(x,r(\xi,\theta)) \setminus X(\xi,L_\xi,\theta)=\varnothing,
		\end{equation}
		where $X(\xi,L_\xi,\theta)$ stands for the closed cone
		$$X(\xi,L_\xi,\theta)= \{x\in{\mathbb R}^{n+1}:{\rm dist}(y,L_\xi) \leq \theta\,|x-\xi|\}.$$
		The existence of tangents for ${\mathcal H}^n$-a.e.\  $\xi\in{\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ follows from the fact that, being ${\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ $n$-rectifiable,
		there exists an approximate tangent for ${\mathcal H}^n$-a.e.\  $\xi\in{\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ (see \cite[Chapter 15]{Mattila}, for example), and then the 
		Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial\Omega}\cup{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ implies that any approximate tangent is also a tangent in the sense above.
		
		For a small $\theta>0$ to be fixed below, let $G_k =\{x\in G: r(x,\theta)\geq 1/k\}$, so that
		$$G = \bigcup_{k\geq1} G_k\cup Z,$$
		with ${\mathcal H}^n(Z)=0$.
		                                                                                                  
		To prove {(\ref{eqnatural1*})}, it suffices
		to show that $\partial_{\nu_A} w(y) = \psi_0(y)$ for $\sigma$-a.e.\ $y\in  G_k$. To this end, we will prove that for any
		compact set $F\subset G_k$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eqigF0}
			\int_F \partial_{\nu_A} w\,d\sigma = \int_F \psi_0\,d\sigma. 
		\end{equation}
		
		For a compact set $F\subset G_k$, let ${\varphi}_{F,\delta}:\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}:\to{\mathbb R}$ be a Lipschitz function such that
		$$\chi_F\leq {\varphi}_{F,\delta}\leq \chi_{U_\delta(F)\cap{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}},$$ where  $U_\delta(F):=\{x \in {\mathbb R}^{n+1}: {\rm dist}(x,F) < \delta\}$ is the $\delta$-neighborhood of $F$. Notice that we have that $F\subset \overline{B}$ because $G_k\subset G\subset \overline{B}$.
		We denote by ${\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ the following Carleson operator, acting over functions or vector fields
		$F:{\widetilde{\Omega}}\to{\mathbb R}$:
		$${\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(F)(\xi) = \sup_{r>0}\frac1{r^n}\int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\cap B(\xi,r)}|F(y)|\,dy,\qquad \xi\in{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}.$$
		
		
		
		\begin{claim}\label{claimff}
			For each $\delta>0$, there exists an extension ${\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}:\overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}\to{\mathbb R}$ of ${\varphi}_{F,\delta}$ which is Lipschitz in 
			$\overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$, such that
			\begin{itemize}
				\item[(a)] $0\leq {\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\leq 1$ and ${\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}$ is supported on $\overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}\cap 3B$, 
				
				\item[(b)] ${\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,\chi_{\partial\Omega} \to\chi_F$ in $L^{q'}(\sigma)$ as $\delta\to0$, and
				
				\item[(c)] $\|{\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\chi_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega}\nabla {\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta})\|_{L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\to 0$ as $\delta\to0$.
			\end{itemize}
		\end{claim}
		
		Assume this claim for the moment and let us see how {(\ref{eqigF0})} follows. By the properties of the Neumann function ${\widetilde{N}}$ and the  definition of $\partial_{\nu_A} w$, we have
		\begin{align}\label{eqal8fv}
			\int_{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}} \psi_0\, {\varphi}_{F,\delta}\,d{\widetilde{\sigma}} & = \int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}} A \nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,dm
			= \int_{\Omega} A \nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,dm + \int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega} A \nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,dm\\
			&= \int_{{\partial\Omega}} \partial_{\nu_A} w\,\,{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,d\sigma + \int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega} A\nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,dm.
			\notag
		\end{align}
		By the definition of ${\varphi}_{F,\delta}$ and by (b) and the fact that $\|\partial_{\nu_A} w\|_{L^q(\sigma|_{2B})}<\infty$, we have, as $\delta\to0$, 
		$$\int_{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}} \psi_0\, {\varphi}_{F,\delta}\,d{\widetilde{\sigma}}\to \int_F \psi_0\, d{\widetilde{\sigma}}\quad \text{ and }\quad
		\int_{{\partial\Omega}} \partial_{\nu_A} w\,{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}\,d\sigma \to \int_F \partial_{\nu_A} w\,d\sigma.$$
		
		To bound the last integral on the right hand side of {(\ref{eqal8fv})} we use the duality result of Hyt\"onen and Ros\'en as proved in \cite[Proposition 2.4]{MPT} (see \cite{HR} for the case when $\Omega={\mathbb R}^{n+1}_+$) and the solvability of $(N_q)_{\mathcal L}$. Indeed, 
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega} |A\nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}|\,dm &\lesssim
			\|{\mathcal N}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\nabla w)\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\,\|{\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\chi_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega}\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta})\|_{L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\\
			&\lesssim \|\psi_0\|_{L^q({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\,\|{\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\chi_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega}\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta})\|_{L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})}.
		\end{align*}
		By (c) in the claim above, $\|{\mathcal C}_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}(\chi_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega}\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta})\|_{L^{q'}({\widetilde{\sigma}})}\to0$
		as $\delta \to 0$, and so 
		$$\int_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega} |\nabla w\,\nabla{\widetilde{{\varphi}}}_{F,\delta}|\,dm \to 0 
		$$
		as $\delta\to0$.
		So letting $\delta\to0$ in the identity {(\ref{eqal8fv})}, we obtain {(\ref{eqigF0})}, which proves the lemma, modulo Claim \ref{claimff}.

body_md:
Consider the Whitney decomposition of ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$ described in Section \ref{secwhitney} and let ${\mathcal W}({\widetilde{\Omega}})$ be the family of Whitney cubes.
		Consider a partition of unity in ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$ with a family of functions $\{\eta_Q\}_{Q\in{\mathcal W}({\widetilde{\Omega}})}$ such that
		$$\chi_{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}=\sum_{Q\in{\mathcal W}({\widetilde{\Omega}})}\eta_Q,$$
		with  $\eta_Q\in C^\infty$, supported 
		on $2Q$, such that $\|\nabla\eta_Q\|_\infty\lesssim 1/\ell(Q)$, for every $Q\in{\mathcal W}({\widetilde{\Omega}})$. For a small $\tau\ll r(B)$ to be chosen below,
		let ${\mathcal W}_\tau({\widetilde{\Omega}})$ be the family of the cubes $Q\in{\mathcal W}({\widetilde{\Omega}})$ such that $\ell(Q)\leq \tau$ and ${\rm dist}(Q,B) \leq \tau$.
		Then we set 
		\begin{equation}\label{eqdefpsif}
			\psi_F= \sum_{Q\in {\mathcal W}_\tau({\widetilde{\Omega}})} m_{b(Q),{\widetilde{\sigma}}}(\chi_F)\,\eta_Q,
		\end{equation}
		where $b(Q)$ is the boundary cube in ${\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$ associated with $Q$ (see Subsection \ref{secwhitney}).
		It is clear that $\psi_F$ satisfies (a). Taking into account that $F\subset B$ and the definition of $\psi_F$, (c) follows easily using
		the Lebesgue differentiation theorem. See \cite[Lemma 3.1]{MZ} for more details, for example.
		
		So it remains to prove the property (b). From the choice of $\tau\ll r(B)$ and the fact that $F\subset B$, it follows that $\operatorname{supp}\psi_F\subset 2B$. So it suffices to
		show that $\operatorname{supp}\psi_F\subset\overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}\cap\overline{\Omega}$ if $\tau$ is taken small enough. First observe that since the 
		cubes $Q\in{\mathcal W}_\tau({\widetilde{\Omega}})$ have side length at most $\tau$, we have that $m_{b(Q),{\widetilde{\sigma}}}(\chi_F)=0$ unless ${\rm dist}(Q,F)\lesssim\tau$. 
		This implies that for some fixed constant $C_9$ (depending on $n$ and the Ahlfors regularity of ${\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$),
		$$\psi_F(x) =0 \quad \mbox{ for all $x\in{\widetilde{\Omega}}$ such that ${\rm dist}(x,F)\geq C_9\tau.$}$$
		
		Let $x_0\in{\widetilde{\Omega}}$ be such that $\psi_F(x_0)\neq0$. Our objective is to prove that $x_0\in \Omega$. Clearly, this implies
		that $\operatorname{supp}(\psi_F)\subset \overline \Omega$.
		Let $\xi\in F$ be such that $|x_0-\xi|={\rm dist}(x_0,F)$.
		By the discussion above, $r:=|x_0-\xi|\leq C_9\tau$. 
		We claim that 
		\begin{equation}\label{eqclaim834}
			({\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega)\cap B(\xi,3r)\subset U_{C\theta r}(L_\xi),
		\end{equation}
		for $\tau$ small enough, where $L_\xi$ is the tangent hyperplane defined in {(\ref{eqtan5})}. Indeed, the condition {(\ref{eqtan5})} ensures that 
		$$({\partial\Omega}\cup {\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}) \cap B(\xi,3r)\subset U_{C\theta r}(L_\xi)$$
		if $3r\leq 1/k$, by the definition of $G_k$. We assume $3C_9\tau\leq 1/k$, so that the preceding condition holds.
		Let $B_\xi^+$, $B_\xi^-$ be the two components of $B(\xi,3r)\setminus U_{C\theta r}(L_\xi)$. By a connectivity argument, any component $B_\xi^\pm$
		is either contained in $\Omega$ or in ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{\Omega}$. By the interior and exterior corkscrew conditions for $\Omega$, if $\theta$ is assumed to be small enough, one component, say $B_\xi^+$, is contained in $\Omega$ and the other, $B_\xi^-$, in ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{\Omega}$. The same argument applies to ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$: one of the components
		$B_\xi^\pm$ is contained in ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$ and the other in ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$. The fact that $\Omega\cap B(\xi,r)\subset{\widetilde{\Omega}}\cap B(\xi,r)$ implies that $B_\xi^+$ is both contained in $\Omega$ and in ${\widetilde{\Omega}}$, while $B_\xi^-$ is contained both in ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{\Omega}$ and in ${\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$.
		It is immediate to check that this implies {(\ref{eqclaim834})}.
		
		Aiming for a contradiction, suppose that $x_0\in{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega$. By {(\ref{eqclaim834})} and the discussion above, $x_0\in U_{C\theta r}(L_\xi)$. Since $B_\xi^-\subset {\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}}$, we deduce that $${\rm dist}(x_0,{\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}) = {\rm dist}(x_0,{\mathbb R}^{n+1}\setminus \overline{{\widetilde{\Omega}}})\leq C\theta r.$$
		For $\theta$ small enough, this implies that if $x_0\in 2Q$ for some $Q\in {\mathcal W}_\tau({\widetilde{\Omega}})$, then 
		$$b(Q)\subset B\big(x_0,\tfrac12r\big)\cap {\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}} \subset {\partial{\widetilde{\Omega}}}\setminus F,$$
		using that $\xi$ is the closest point from $F$ to $x_0$ and that $r=|x_0-\xi|$ for the last inclusion.
		Consequently, $m_{b(Q),{\widetilde{\sigma}}}(\chi_F)=0$, and so $\psi_F(x_0)=0$ by the definition of $\psi_F$ in {(\ref{eqdefpsif})}.
		This contradicts the assumption that $\psi_F(x_0)\neq0$, and thus $x_0\not\in{\widetilde{\Omega}}\setminus\Omega$.
